chapters.file: ch08 - First Quarter Football’S Lessons For the Game Of Life.md
ch09 - Vince Lombardi and the Philosophy of Winning.md
chapters.relation: Belliotti reconstructs Vince Lombardi's 'winning isn't everything, it's the only thing' as a deeper philosophy of pursuing excellence and perfection as process values, not victory as such. He rebuts Marxist charges (via Sage) that competitive sport is mere capitalist superstructure by arguing, with Marx and Nietzsche, that hard creative labor and self-overcoming are human goods in themselves rather than mere capitalist demands. Lombardi is cast as a 'grand transcender' whose danger of fascism arises only when winning becomes an end in itself.

Fry uses fumbles—Tony Romo's botched hold, Jerome Bettis's near-disaster saved by Roethlisberger, Leon Lett's showboating—as psychodramas illustrating the fragility of the good life. He invokes Aristotle's worry that one cannot call a life happy until it is complete, and Thomas Nagel's 'moral luck' (the negligent truck driver) to argue our culpability for fumbling, on the field and in life, is shaped by contingency, so responses should be discriminating. He draws on Frankfurt on caring and closes on redemption through effort, luck, and grace.

chapters.file: ch11 - Football and Aristotle'S Philosophy of Friendship.md
chapters.relation: Gallagher maps Aristotle's three kinds of philia onto football: friendship of utility (the quarterback needing his offensive linemen), of pleasure (Friday-night high school and college ball), and of shared goodness (Bo Schembechler's bond with Anthony Carter, who deflected reporters to teammates). He reads the Steelers dynasty and Paterno's locker-room 'love' through Aristotle's 'concord' and 'a single soul in two bodies,' and answers Bertrand Russell's worry about violent competition by insisting football is grounded in philia, not enmity.

chapters.file: ch12 - Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know.md
chapters.relation: Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.

chapters.file: ch13 - Second Quarter Playing Well Between the Lines.md

chapters.relation: Parker asks what pleases football fans and argues the answer is beauty, framed around a Michael Vick scramble against the Ravens. He applies Kant's Critique of Judgment—beauty as disinterested, an end in itself, and its judgments nonconceptual yet universal ('you should too')—to explain why fans watch games rather than read box scores, and why skilled offensive play by Barry Sanders or Joe Montana strikes us as beautiful. Using Ted Cohen's 'circles of taste' and an informal survey, he concludes beauty admits of degree and depends on the viewer's grasp of context.

chapters.file: ch15 - Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person.md
chapters.relation: Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.

chapters.file: ch16 - What's so Bad about Performance-Enhancing Drugs.md
chapters.relation: Ryan evaluates three arguments that using performance-enhancing drugs is wrong, drawing on cases like Barry Bonds, Lyle Alzado, and Ben Johnson. The Against-the-Rules argument shows only that PED use breaks current rules, not that it should be banned; the Unfairness argument overgeneralizes, since sport is full of tolerated unfairness (better coaching, nutrition, natural gifts); and the Harm-and-Pressure argument turns on empirical facts and a paternalism-versus-autonomy debate about whether adults may choose the risk. She concludes no argument yet establishes that PEDs ought to be banned as inherently wrong.

chapters.file: ch17 - The True Nature of Cheating.md
chapters.relation: Swain and Brand build a definition of cheating by successive counterexamples set in a fictional State-versus-Central championship. They move from breaking a formal rule for unfair advantage, to including informal conventions (the hypothetical pre-rule Bonds steroid case), to 'enhancing one's chances of winning' (a coach fielding ineligible players to level the field), and finally add a defeasibility clause so that convention-sanctioned tactics like running out the play clock are not cheating. Trash-talking within the rules is classed as gamesmanship, not cheating.

chapters.file: ch18 - “They Don't Pay Nobody to Be Humble!” Football's Ego Problem.md
chapters.relation: Holowchak diagnoses football's ego problem—Keyshawn Johnson's deactivation, Terrell Owens's self-promotion, Deion Sanders's showboating—as fed by sensationalism (via Dewey) and statistical obsession that pull players out of the team framework. He proposes 'Aretism,' a modern progressivist ethics built on Stoic oikeiosis (Chrysippus, Cicero, Seneca, Epictetus and Hierokles's concentric circles) balancing self- and other-concern, and on Kant's injunction to treat others as ends. The virtuous athlete competes fully while respecting opponents, sport, and the 'moral zone' of Stoic sagacity.

chapters.file: ch19 - Third Quarter Philosophical Armchair Quarterbacking.md
ch20 - Crowning a True Champion The Case for a College Football Playoff.md
chapters.relation: Austin argues the BCS is unjust and that a sixteen-team college football playoff should decide the champion on the field, using the undefeated 2006 Boise State Broncos as his key case. He applies a merit-based principle of distributive justice, taking 'victory on the field' rather than economic contribution as the appropriate basis of desert, and invokes Robert Simon's ideal of athletic competition as 'a mutual quest for excellence through challenge.' He answers BCS defenders and academic-integrity worries (Gordon Gee) by proposing reforms that let sport enhance the university's mission.

Reid draws an extended analogy between big-time college football players and Roman gladiators—both socially marginalized entertainers, controlled by coaches/editors and crowds, risking their bodies for others' entertainment. Through Roman Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Cicero) she argues virtus does not depend on external wealth, status, or freedom but on accepting fate and excelling within one's role, so exploited athletes can still be genuine heroes of virtue. Following Marcus Aurelius's distaste for the games, she concludes those with power over players' unjust conditions are morally obliged to improve them.

Kershnar analyzes what makes a football player valuable, arguing a player's value is his net benefit to his own team measured against a baseline. He compares three models—no-substitute, average/reasonable-substitute, and actual-substitute—using cases like Joe Montana backed by Steve Young and Emmitt Smith behind an all-pro line, and defends the actual-substitute model as the correct measure of value even though it yields counterintuitive results. He connects the account to a broader question of measuring a person's contribution to any organization or to the world.

chapters.file: ch23 - Upon Further Review Instant Replay Is an All-or-Nothing Affair.md
chapters.relation: Smith argues that consistency in applying rules and their motivations forces instant replay to be all-or-nothing: either every play is reviewable or none is. He shows the two rationales—'get the calls right' and 'preserve the flow of the game'—each apply to all plays, then dismantles the reviewable/nonreviewable line by arguing neither the 'judgment call' distinction (goal-line and fumble calls are judgment-laden, field goals are not) nor the 'correctable call' distinction (every play is correctable, e.g. via replaying the down) can hold, using the Roethlisberger Super Bowl XL touchdown as a case.

chapters.file: ch24 - Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League.md
chapters.relation: Collins-Cavanaugh presents the NFL salary cap as a model of utilitarian distributive justice via Mill's greatest happiness principle: owners and fans gain (guaranteed revenue and a fairer, more competitive league) while players lose relatively little. He then tests empirically—competitive-balance scores, playoff berths, championship distribution, and comparison to MLB and the NBA—and finds little evidence the cap actually increases fairness. Because the claimed fan happiness is not genuinely caused by the cap, the utilitarian justification collapses, leaving only the players' net loss against the owners' gain.

chapters.file: ch26 - Is the Gridiron Holy Ground.md
chapters.relation: Hamilton analyzes the fusion of football, patriotism, and religion (Friday Night Lights' Odessa, Super Bowl rituals) as Rousseau's 'civil religion' from the Social Contract—socially unifying but content-empty and anti-intellectual, keeping faith bifurcated from real life. Drawing on Augustine's account of virtue as 'rightly ordered love' and vice as disordered love, he argues football has been wrongly elevated above higher goods. He rejects Higgs's incompatibility thesis for a Christian worldview approach—exemplified by Tony Dungy, Lovie Smith, and Joe Ehrman's 'men for others'—that makes the gridiron holy ground.

Campbell applies the truthmaker theory and correspondence theory of truth to 'touchdown truths,' using plays like Devin Hester's opening kickoff return in Super Bowl XLI. He distinguishes truthbearers (propositions) from truthmakers (events), separates an agent's 'making it the case' from a truthmaker's 'necessitating,' and uses a tenseless view of semantics plus Perry's being-true/being-made-true distinction to defuse fatalism. He then argues that since only the final score fixes 'real' touchdowns, their truthmakers are events involving referees' beliefs, endorsing a Modest Touchdown Antirealism while retaining bivalence and semantic realism.

Letson asks whether momentum in football is a real explanatory phenomenon, opening with the Bills' 1993 comeback over the Oilers. He notes momentum is invoked only for success and only for one team at a time, and struggles to separate it from the mere evidence of playing well, comparing it to 'talent.' Surveying psychological models (Taylor and Demick's momentum chain) and David Romer's fourth-down analysis denying momentum, he argues that even if a small momentum effect exists, its size relative to chance means appeals to it in any particular game are usually unjustified—like blaming one heart attack on smoking.
